questions.prompt: Why is 'encryption is the end of an intrusion, not the beginning' the central reframe of this playbook?
options: Because encryption is always the attacker's first action
Because the attacker has usually been present for days or weeks first, so the investigation runs backwards and initial access determines whether recovery holds
Because encrypted files cannot be analyzed
Because ransomware never involves lateral movement
questions.explanation: Treating encryption as the start of the incident misses the preceding access, lateral movement, and often exfiltration -- and leads to restoring into an environment the attacker still holds.

questions.prompt: Why does the playbook favor network isolation over powering off affected hosts?
options: Network isolation stops the spread while preserving memory evidence that power-off destroys
Powered-off systems cannot be restored from backup
questions.explanation: Both stop lateral encryption, but power-off also destroys volatile memory containing process state, network connections, and sometimes keys.

questions.prompt: Why does determining exfiltration belong in the first hour rather than later?
options: Exfiltration evidence is only available for 60 minutes
Double extortion may make exfiltration the greater problem, changing notification obligations, legal exposure, and negotiation posture entirely
It is required before backups can be restored
Exfiltration always precedes encryption by exactly one hour
questions.explanation: Whether data left changes the legal and business shape of the entire incident, so it cannot be deferred until after technical recovery is underway.

questions.prompt: Why is restoring from backup risky before initial access is identified?
options: Backups are always corrupted during ransomware
If you cannot say when initial access occurred, you cannot say whether your restore point is already compromised
Backups can only be restored once
questions.explanation: A restore point predating discovery may still postdate initial access, returning the environment to a state the attacker already controlled -- the common path to re-encryption.
